I'm Lena Verbruggen, twenty-two years old, and I've lived in Antwerp my whole life — specifically in the Borgerhout district, in a narrow three-story row house my parents bought in 2009 that always smelled faintly of rust and bread. My father, Pieter, worked as a structural welder at the Port of Antwerp for over two decades, so the smell of hot metal was basically my childhood. By the time I was sixteen I was spending weekends in his workshop watching him shape steel, and at eighteen I enrolled in a two-year vocational program at the Provinciale Technische School in Mechelen, about thirty kilometres south of home. I graduated in June 2022 and landed my current job within three months — I work as an industrial blacksmith at Debacker & Zonen, a mid-sized forging company on the Industrieweg in the Haven Noord area of Antwerp. I mostly fabricate custom brackets, hinges, and structural reinforcement components for the maritime and construction sectors. The forge temperature I work with most days sits around 1,200 degrees Celsius, and I still feel a small thrill every time I pull a piece of glowing steel out of the furnace.

My health has shaped my daily life in ways people don't always expect. I was diagnosed with celiac disease at age fourteen after a miserable year of stomach cramps and fatigue that my GP kept dismissing as stress. Once I finally saw a gastroenterologist at the UZA hospital and got the diagnosis, I had to overhaul everything I ate. I can't tolerate even trace amounts of gluten, so I cook almost all my own meals — a rice or buckwheat base most nights, and I've become surprisingly good at making gluten-free stroopwafels from scratch. Eating out in Antwerp takes research, but there are a handful of places I trust, including a small café on the Kloosterstraat called De Groene Peer that labels everything meticulously.

Outside work, I train jujitsu three evenings a week at a club called Zandvliet Martial Arts, which is technically a fifteen-minute bike ride from my house. I started at age fifteen and received my blue belt in March 2023. My instructor, Sensei Wouter Claes, has been training for over thirty years and runs the club with his wife. I genuinely love the technical problem-solving aspect of ground work — it feels not entirely unlike the precision required at the forge.

My other obsession is vinyl. I collect jazz records, and my current collection sits at around 140 albums stored in two wooden crates under my bed. My most prized possession is a 1959 original Blue Note pressing of John Coltrane's 'Giant Steps' that I found at a flea market in the Vrijdagmarkt square for twelve euros — a price the seller clearly regretted when I got home and looked it up. I play records on a Pro-Ject Debut Carbon turntable I bought secondhand from a colleague in 2021. Miles Davis, Thelonious Monk, and Chet Baker are my most-played artists. There's something about putting on a record after a long day at the forge — hands still a little sore, the needle dropping into the groove — that resets everything.

I was born in 1982 in Ghent, but my family moved to Antwerp when I was seven, and I've been rooted here ever since. I live in a narrow three-storey townhouse on Lange Leemstraat, just close enough to the Rubenshuis that tourists occasionally ring my bell thinking I'm part of the museum district. I'm 42 now, and I've spent the last eighteen years running a small calligraphy studio I named Inktlijn — it started as a hobby desk in my spare bedroom and grew into a proper workspace on the ground floor where I do wedding invitations, corporate lettering commissions, and the occasional book title for a publisher in Brussels.

I discovered calligraphy at twenty-four when a friend dragged me to a weekend workshop at the Academie voor Schone Kunsten here in Antwerp. The instructor, a German woman named Hildegard Breuer, handed me a broad-edged nib and a sheet of practice paper, and within an hour I knew this was not a passing interest. I bought my first proper calligraphy set — a Brause kit I still have — the very next morning.

The crossword constructing came later, around 2015, when I started solving puzzles obsessively during slow winter months. Within a year I'd shifted to constructing them. I've had nine grids accepted by De Standaard, which still feels absurd to me. There's a satisfaction in locking together a 15-by-15 grid that rhymes, strangely, with the satisfaction of completing a page of Italic script — both are systems governed by invisible constraints you have to feel before you can see.

The motorcycle side of my life is messier and louder. I own two Triumph motorcycles: a 1969 Bonneville T120 that I bought in pieces from an estate sale in Mechelen in 2011, and a 1974 Tiger 100 I found through a club contact in Rotterdam in 2019. The Bonneville took me three years to restore — I sourced the correct Amal carburetors from a specialist in Coventry after exhausting every Belgian lead. I'm a member of the Antwerp Vintage Riders club, and we do a summer run every July that ends, depending on the weather, somewhere in the Ardennes.

The celiac disease was diagnosed in 2008 after two years of being told I had irritable bowel syndrome. It reorganized my kitchen entirely. I am a reasonably skilled cook now by sheer necessity. I make my own sourdough from a rice-and-buckwheat starter I've maintained since 2010. Belgian beer culture, which is almost a civic religion here, is something I navigate carefully — I keep a short list of lambics and dedicated-facility ciders that I trust. Anything brewed on shared equipment is a gamble I stopped taking.

I am not married, though I was briefly engaged in my early thirties. I have a grey whippet named Quill — the name was perhaps inevitable — who sleeps under my drafting table most days and has strong opinions about the hours I keep. My best friend, Pieter Vandermeersch, teaches medieval history at the University of Antwerp and is the person most likely to beat me at my own crosswords, which I find both annoying and deeply reassuring.

I was born in 1959 in Dundee, Scotland, the third of four children in a family that spent every summer camping near Loch Rannoch. My father, a veterinarian named Alistair Drummond, would drag injured foxes and hedgehogs home regularly, which is probably why animals never felt foreign to me. I was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes at age nine, in 1968, which meant my childhood was punctuated by insulin injections and careful meal planning — but it never stopped me from roaming the hills with a compass and a rucksack.

I moved to Marrakech in 1997 after spending eight years working for an animal welfare NGO based in Nairobi. I had intended to stay in Morocco for only two years, but I fell completely in love with the Atlas Mountain foothills and ended up buying a small property in the Ourika Valley, about 35 kilometres south of the city centre. My riad has a converted outbuilding that I use as a rehabilitation enclosure for injured Barbary macaques, Egyptian mongooses, and the occasional hedgehog — the long-eared Algerian hedgehog, specifically, which is far more common out here than most people realise.

I founded the Ourika Wildlife Refuge in 2003 with a starting budget of roughly 14,000 dirhams, money I had saved from freelance consulting work. We are now a licensed facility with three part-time Moroccan staff and a revolving roster of European volunteers. Since opening, we have released over 800 animals back into the wild, a number I keep painted on a wooden sign above the enclosure door — it needs updating almost monthly.

My amateur radio hobby began in 2005 when a neighbour named Rachid gave me a decommissioned Yaesu FT-817 transceiver. I obtained my Moroccan licence the following year under the callsign CN8QD, and I now operate mostly on the 40-metre and 20-metre bands, often making contact with fellow operators in the Canary Islands and southern Spain. Radio is enormously useful during the flash floods that occasionally cut off the valley road; I can relay information to the emergency services in Marrakech when mobile networks fail.

The bagpipes are harder to explain to my Moroccan neighbours. I started learning as a teenager at Dundee's Morgan Academy, playing with the school pipe band from age 14. I brought my Fraser & Sons chanter and full set of pipes with me when I moved, and I still practise in the courtyard most Saturday mornings. The sound carries remarkably far in the valley and has, over the years, attracted curious goatherds, baffled tourists, and at least one very startled Barbary macaque who needed re-catching.

Managing type 1 diabetes in a region with unreliable electricity and occasional supply chain disruptions is genuinely challenging. I use an insulin pump — a Medtronic model I have been on since 2011 — and I keep a three-month insulin reserve stored in a small generator-backed refrigerator. My endocrinologist, Dr Fatima Benali at the Clinique du Sud in Marrakech, sees me every four months and has been my physician since 2009. I do not let the condition define my days, but I do not ignore it either. At 65, I find that the rhythm of caring for injured animals, tinkering with radio equipment, and blowing air through a bag of Scottish pipes is the finest possible medicine for a body that requires a certain amount of daily vigilance.

I'm Callum Ouzzani, and I'll be 66 in March — 66 years of a life that has taken more unexpected turns than any crossword I've ever built. I was born on March 14, 1959, in Inverness, Scotland, to a Scottish father and a Moroccan mother from Fès, which explains the surname that confuses everyone I meet. We moved to Marrakech when I was eleven, after my father, a civil engineer named Douglas Ouzzani, took a contract rebuilding irrigation infrastructure in the Haouz plain. I never went back to live in Scotland, though I visit my cousin Fiona in Nairn every few summers.

I've worked as a park ranger in the Toubkal National Park since 1991 — thirty-three years now, longer than some of my colleagues have been alive. The park covers roughly 380 square kilometres in the High Atlas mountains, and I know most of it the way other men know their living rooms. My official base is the ranger station just outside Imlil village, about 60 kilometres south of Marrakech, but I rent a small apartment in the Guéliz neighbourhood of Marrakech itself, on Rue Ibn Aicha, where I spend my days off. I was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes in 1987, when I was 28, and managing insulin at altitude in variable temperatures took years of hard-won discipline. I carry a glucose meter and two spare insulin pens in a small insulated pouch strapped to my belt every single shift.

The bagpipes came back into my life in 2003. My father had taught me the basics on a practice chanter as a child, but I'd abandoned it for decades. A Scottish tourist left a set of Highland pipes at the ranger station — genuinely forgot them on a group trek — and never came back to collect them. After six months I put up notices, heard nothing, and simply kept them. I now practice for at least forty-five minutes every evening on the roof terrace of my apartment. My neighbours in Guéliz have a complicated relationship with this habit.

The crossword constructing is the more solitary obsession. I began submitting puzzles to Al-Araby magazine in 2011, and by 2014 I had won their annual constructors' competition twice. I work exclusively in Arabic for that outlet, but I also construct English-language puzzles that I submit to a small syndicate based in Dublin called GridIron Puzzles Ltd., which distributes to about forty regional newspapers. My grids are always 15×15 and I refuse to use computer-generation software — every clue written by hand in a set of graph-paper notebooks I buy from a stationery shop called Bouzid Papeterie near the Koutoubia Mosque. I currently have fourteen completed notebooks on my shelf.

Life here is unglamorous and entirely mine. I eat lunch most days at a small restaurant called Chez Brahim on the edge of the medina that does a lamb tagine I've been ordering since 2006. I drink my coffee without sugar — obviously — and I sleep well, mostly, when my blood sugar behaves. I am not lonely. I am exactly where I belong.

Within six months I had bought my first serious bearing-equipped yo-yo, a titanium Recess First Base modified with custom axle work, and I started entering regional competitions. Friends think it's macabre; I think it's a form of respect for the animal and a meditation on structure beneath surface — which, come to think of it, is exactly what cooking is.

I compete in sheepdog trials with my two Border Collies, Nessa and Fig. Nessa is six years old and has been my serious trial dog since she was about eighteen months; she and I placed second at the 2022 Northern Thailand Working Dog Association trials held outside Chiang Rai, which remains my proudest competitive result to date. Fig is only two and still learning the finer points of shedding. Finding actual sheep to work with in Chiang Mai is an ongoing logistical puzzle — I rent time with a small flock owned by a farmer named Khun Boonlert in Mae Rim, about 22 kilometers from my house, and we go out there every Saturday morning without fail.

Beyond the dogs, I brew kombucha at home in ceramic crocks I sourced from a pottery village near Lampang. I maintain three active SCOBY cultures at any given time and currently have a 19-liter batch of ginger-turmeric blend fermenting in my kitchen. I started brewing about five years ago partly out of necessity — I was diagnosed with celiac disease in 2019, which forced me to overhaul my entire diet and cut gluten completely. That diagnosis was a difficult adjustment, particularly in Thailand where soy sauce is in nearly everything, but it ultimately pushed me toward fermenting and cooking from scratch, which I now love.

I also volunteer with the Chiang Mai Mountain Rescue Unit, a group of about 35 volunteers that operates primarily in the Doi Inthanon and Doi Suthep-Pui national park areas. I completed my wilderness first responder certification through a course run in January 2021 in Pai, and I've participated in fourteen documented search-and-rescue operations since joining the unit in late 2020. Nessa occasionally comes on operations where a dog's tracking instincts are useful, though she isn't formally certified as a SAR dog — that certification process is something I'm actively exploring for her.

My house in Hang Dong is a modest two-story concrete and teak structure with a large walled garden where the dogs have room to run. I grow rosemary, Thai basil, and two varieties of chili along the south wall. Every weekday morning I drive a 2018 Honda PCX scooter to a language school in Nimman where I teach English to adult professional students — it's not what I trained for, but it pays reliably and I genuinely enjoy it. I stay in touch with a sheepdog handler community mostly online through a forum called Border Collie Connect, where I've been an active member since 2010, long before my Thailand chapter began. I never expected to end up back in school at 47, but here I am, halfway through a Master's degree in oceanography at the University of Saskatchewan in Saskatoon. I grew up in Dartmouth, Nova Scotia, right across the harbour from Halifax, which is probably where my obsession with the ocean began. My father worked on a container vessel for Oceanex Shipping, so saltwater was practically in my blood. But life took me inland — I spent nearly two decades working as a land surveyor for a municipal engineering firm called TriSpec Solutions in Regina, where I clocked in every day from 2004 until 2021. The work paid well and I was good at it, but after my divorce in 2019 I found myself reassessing everything. I sold the house on Wascana Drive and used part of the proceeds to finally go back to school.

I enrolled at U of S in January 2022, focusing my research on sediment transport in Arctic coastal systems. My supervisor, Dr. Lena Marchetti, is one of the foremost people in Canada working on permafrost-adjacent shoreline erosion, and I feel genuinely lucky to have landed in her lab. My thesis is looking specifically at sediment flux rates along the Mackenzie Delta, and I'm planning a field season up near Inuvik this coming August.

Living in Saskatoon on a graduate stipend of $21,000 a year after nearly two decades of a surveyor's salary has required serious adjustment. I rent a one-bedroom apartment on Avenue P South for $975 a month, which is manageable, but there isn't much left over. I do most of my own cooking, which is non-negotiable anyway because I was diagnosed with celiac disease in 2017. That diagnosis changed my relationship with food completely — I've become a competent enough baker using rice flour and tapioca blends, and I know every gluten-free-friendly restaurant in the city by heart.

Disc golf keeps me sane. There's a solid 18-hole course at Diefenbaker Park that I play at least twice a week when the weather cooperates, which in Saskatchewan means roughly May through October. I throw a Discraft Buzzz as my go-to midrange disc and have been slowly working my handicap down. I joined the Saskatoon Disc Golf Club in the spring of 2022 and have made a few genuinely good friends there, mostly people a decade younger than me who seem unbothered by having a middle-aged oceanography student tagging along.

I also race with a dragon boat team called the Prairie Paddlers, which sounds incongruous for a landlocked city but there's actually a vibrant paddling community on the South Saskatchewan River. We practice on Tuesday and Thursday evenings from June through September at the Rotary Park boat launch. Our team finished third in the recreational division at the Saskatchewan Dragon Boat Festival in 2023, which felt like a genuine achievement given we'd only been together as a crew for about fourteen months.

I don't know exactly what I'll do with this degree. Maybe federal fisheries work, maybe something with the Department of Oceans and Climate up north. But for the first time since my twenties, I feel like I'm pointed in the right direction.

I came to Canada in 2008 from Busan, South Korea, when I was seventeen years old, landing first in Toronto before eventually making my way west. My parents had hoped I'd study engineering or medicine — something practical — but I enrolled in the Visual Arts program at the University of Victoria in 2009, where a second-year typography class taught by Professor David Lam changed everything for me. He brought in a set of 19th-century metal type slugs and let us hand-set a single line of text. I pressed my palm against the inked forme and felt the slight resistance, and I knew then that I wanted to spend my life doing exactly this kind of work.

I graduated in 2013 with a degree in Visual Arts, concentrating in printmaking, and stayed in Victoria rather than returning to Busan or moving to Vancouver. I rent a small house on Fern Street near the Fernwood neighbourhood, with a detached garage I've converted into a proper studio. The centrepiece of that studio is a 1962 Chandler & Price platen press I bought in 2017 from a retired printer in Duncan, BC, for $2,400. Getting it through the garage door required three friends, a furniture dolly, and language I don't normally use. I do letterpress printing alongside my calligraphy commissions — mostly wedding invitations, certificates, and limited-edition broadsides for local poets.

Calligraphy itself I've been practising seriously since 2010, when I started studying with a local master named Hiroko Tanaka, who runs a small studio in James Bay. She specialises in Western scripts — Copperplate, Italic, and Uncial — and I trained with her for four years before branching out on my own. My preferred script now is Spencerian, which I find more forgiving and expressive than Copperplate. I use a Nikko G nib for most of my client work, though for personal projects I keep a small stock of vintage Gillott 303 nibs I order from a supplier in the UK.

I've been brewing kombucha since 2015, partly as a way to keep my hands occupied during the long stretches when I'm waiting for ink to dry. My continuous-brew vessel holds four litres and I maintain two SCOBYs — one original culture I've had since the beginning and a backup I keep at a friend's house in case of disaster. My current favourite flavour combination is ginger with a small amount of dried hibiscus, which gives it a colour I can only describe as the inside of a garnet. I bottle on Sundays, without exception, and I trade bottles with neighbours in exchange for vegetables from their gardens.

Being a first-generation immigrant informs the work in ways I'm still figuring out. I sometimes incorporate Hangul letterforms into decorative borders or use them as structural counterpoints to Roman scripts. I sold a series of twelve prints combining Hangul and Italic script at the Victoria Public Market in November 2022, and every piece sold within two hours. That was the first time I felt the two parts of my identity were genuinely speaking to each other rather than competing. I turned 34 in March of this year, and I'm slowly putting together a solo exhibition I'd like to open by autumn.

I was born in Bergen on March 14, 1959, and I have lived here my entire life — I cannot imagine waking up anywhere without the smell of the North Sea and the sound of rain on the Bryggen wharf. I still have that camera on a shelf in my studio on Øvregaten Street, though it no longer works properly.

Over the decades I have photographed well over 900 weddings, but the one that stays with me most was a winter ceremony at Fantoft Stave Church in December 2003, where the light through the snow was unlike anything I had ever seen before or since. I use a Sony A7R V now for my professional work, though I will admit that film still makes my heart beat a little faster.

My mother was Dutch and my father Norwegian, which meant I grew up speaking both Norwegian and Dutch at the kitchen table. I added English in school, as every Norwegian child does, and then I spent a year living in Seville in 1984 before I started the photography business, learning Spanish well enough to hold real conversations. Four languages total — Norwegian, Dutch, English, and Spanish — and I am proud of all of them, even if my Spanish has grown rusty since my last visit to Andalusia in 2019.

People are always surprised by my hobbies. About fifteen years ago, around 2009, I discovered sport lock picking through a club in Oslo called Åpen Hengelås — which roughly translates to Open Padlock. I drive down to Oslo three or four times a year for their meetups, and I have won second place in their annual precision picking competition twice, in 2014 and 2018. I keep a practice board in my living room with fourteen different locks mounted on it, ranging from a basic Master Lock No. 3 to a Abloy Protec2 that has defeated me for going on two years now.

The other hobby most people find bizarre is competitive whistling. I have been doing it since I was a teenager, but I only entered my first formal competition in 1997 at a Nordic folk music festival in Voss, about 60 kilometers east of Bergen. I specialize in what the community calls artistic whistling — melodic pieces rather than volume or endurance — and Edvard Grieg's 'In the Hall of the Mountain King' is my signature piece, which feels appropriate given that I live in Bergen. I have placed in the top three at Voss three times over the years.

I live alone now in a red wooden house in the Sandviken neighborhood with my dog, a grey Norwegian Elkhound named Brage.
